title: Standard Model Nuclear Physics May Explain Dark Energy and Cosmic Expansion
excerpt: Astrophysicists propose that dark energy driving cosmic expansion may naturally originate from the quantum vacuum of the strong nuclear force within the Standard Model.
content:
One of cosmology’s greatest mysteries may be explained by the known laws of particle physics, according to new research by astrophysicists at the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield. In a peer-reviewed study published in the Astrophysical Journal, the researchers propose that dark energy, the mysterious component driving the accelerating expansion of the cosmos, may originate from the same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together. Their theoretical framework suggests that the observed cosmic acceleration might be accounted for directly within the Standard Model of particle physics, potentially removing the need to introduce hypothetical new fields or undetected particles.

For nearly three decades, scientists have struggled to explain how dark energy operates. Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 per cent of the universe’s total energy budget, exerting an enormous influence across cosmic evolution, yet physicists still do not know what it is or where it comes from. In contrast, the new work indicates that the phenomenon might instead be explained by Quantum Chromodynamics, the well-established theoretical framework describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons.

The study focuses on the intricate quantum properties of seemingly empty space. In Quantum Chromodynamics, the vacuum is not void but a complex environment packed with subatomic fields and quantum energy possessing topological properties that can influence space across vast distances. The University of British Columbia researchers proposed that as the universe expands, this subatomic vacuum structure responds differently over time. This ongoing evolution produces an energy shift sufficiently powerful to drive cosmic acceleration naturally, without introducing any new fundamental particles into physics.

According to the theoretical model, the characteristic energy scale predicted from the combination of gravity and the Quantum Chromodynamics vacuum aligns closely with the dark energy scale observed today. Professor Ariel Zhitnitsky of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of British Columbia, whose theoretical concepts provided the basis for the paper, noted that no ad-hoc new fields or arbitrary parameters are required. Professor Ludovic Van Waerbeke added that the most striking aspect of the result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants without requiring additional fitting parameters.

Researchers at the University of Sheffield collaborated with the Canadian team to evaluate the theoretical framework directly against observational cosmological data. Dong Ha Lee, a PhD researcher at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the paper, highlighted that testing models based on this mechanism against observational data is an essential step. The team’s analysis confirmed that their Quantum Chromodynamics vacuum model successfully reproduces the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations, providing a strong motivation for further theoretical study into how quantum vacuum structures respond to cosmic expansion.

To assess its performance against standard cosmology, the researchers tested the model against real astronomical observations. These benchmarks included measurements of light emitted by distant exploding supernovae and leftover cosmic radiation originating from the early universe. The model matched these observational datasets just as effectively as conventional cosmological frameworks, while uniquely providing a grounded physical origin for dark energy within existing particle physics.

Looking ahead, the authors plan to refine their theoretical calculations and verify the framework against upcoming observational data. Next-generation space telescopes are scheduled to deliver unprecedented precision and detail regarding the history and expansion of the universe over the coming years, offering critical observational tests for whether standard nuclear physics truly accounts for the accelerating cosmos.
